newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Piedmont faces fight with Olivetti.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Piedmont faces fight with Olivetti.

text.p: Italy's Piedmont faces an uphill struggle in turning around the ailing fortunes of Olivetti's PC business, industry analysts said on Thursday.

With the world computer industry consolidating rapidly and the European industry littered with the failures of famous names, they questioned how a small leverage buyout firm can succeed where others have failed.
In order to survive, analysts said Piedmont needs global alliances, a jump in volumes and updated products.

On Monday, Olivetti's chief executive Roberto Colaninno fulfilled a promise to quit personal computers and offloaded the company to Piedmont International, a consortium brought together by U.S. lawyer Edward Gottesman.

Olivetti's PC business lost its way in the early 1990s under an onslaught from low-cost U.S. and Far East makers. The Italian group simply could not get its costs down quick enough to compete and it failed to achieve a real global presence.

But most industry analysts were puzzled over how a company specialising in turning around relative low-tech businesses like bicycle-maker Raleigh and fine porclein group Royal Worcester in Britain could restore a leading-edge technology company in a massively competitive market.
"I'm mystified as to how they can make a return on this business, there must be another bit to the equation that we do not know about yet," said one leading industry analyst.

Piedmont is acquiring Olivetti's PC business for 250-300 billion lire ($160-190 million). Italian industrialist Gianmario Rossignolo, who is chairman of Electrolux's Zanussi unit, has agreed to run the venture while former Olivetti PC managing director Bernhard Auer stays on.

"This is a tough game for Piedmont to resolve. There are plenty of question to ask. What is their strategy? how aggressive will they be on overseas distribution? and how will they update their products on offer?," said another analyst.

The PC business lost 200 billion lire in 1995 and in the first half of 1996 made an operating loss of 10 billion lire. The swing in losses has perplexed analysts who say a lot depends on the price at which PCs were sold to other parts of Olivetti.
Therefore, much depends on the details of an agreement under which Piedmont will sell PCs to Olivetti's systems and services company.

Analysts said that Olivetti had brought about efficiencies by cutting staff numbers to around 1,600 recently, but they still did not know how efficient the manufacturing process was and whether there was potential for Piedmont to improve management.

Olivetti PCs has struggled to make profit in the 1990s, and analysts said it was unlikely to have reached annual sales of 800,000 PCs required to breakeven in 1996. Estimates put sales at only just over 700,000.

They pointed out 95 percent of Olivetti PCs were sold in Europe, and around one third in Italy. So the company needs a partner from the U.S. or the Far East to give it the global spread to compete with U.S. giants like IBM and Compaq.

One analyst said that the company had to improve its product offer and overcome some views in the marketplace that Olivetti was struggling to keep up with launching new up-to-date products in an extremely fast-moving market.

European PC makers have dwindled in recent years with the only true indigenous PC manufacturer remaining being German Siemens Nixdorf. France's Bull, Britain's ICL and Germany's Vobis have all been in retreat.

"This is a company that has turned around Raleigh and Royal Worcestor, but it is difficult to see Piedmont making a go of Olivetti PCs in an industry where so many have pulled back or simply given up," said one Milan-based analyst.
Analysts said that Piedmont probably took on 200 billion lire of debt in buying the PC company, and is likely to be buying a company with an equity value of 60-65 billion lire. ($1=1,600 lire)
